filtered_findings.description: unpack_mqtt_connect() copies an attacker-controlled 16-bit client-ID length into the fixed 64-byte `client_id[MQTT_CLIENT_ID_LEN]` array without any bound check (also writes a NUL at client_id[cid_len]). The destination lives inside `struct mqtt_packet`, which is embedded in `struct io_event` allocated on the stack in process_message(), so any remote client can smash the stack (and the adjacent union/heap-adjacent data) with a CONNECT packet, before any authentication is performed.
filtered_findings.exploit_scenario: An unauthenticated TCP client sends a CONNECT packet whose payload declares client-id length 300-65535 and supplies that many bytes. mqtt_unpack() -> unpack_mqtt_connect() does memcpy(pkt->connect.payload.client_id, buf, cid_len) past the end of the 64-byte field. This was reproduced locally against the built broker under ASan: a single packet ('TEST2') produced 'AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow ... in unpack_mqtt_connect src/mqtt.c:240' and killed the broker (SEGV). Because the overflow is on the pre-auth path and attacker-controlled, it is memory corruption with RCE potential, not merely a crash.
filtered_findings.recommendation: Reject CONNECT packets where cid_len >= MQTT_CLIENT_ID_LEN (and validate that the declared remaining length actually contains the field) before copying, e.g. `if (cid_len >= sizeof(pkt->connect.payload.client_id) || cid_len > len - consumed) return -MQTT_ERR;`. Also bounds-check the will/username/password length reads against the remaining packet length.

_filter_metadata.justification: This is C code (not Rust, so the memory-safety exclusion does not apply). The finding describes a concrete, pre-authentication stack buffer overflow: an attacker-controlled 16-bit client-ID length is memcpy'd into a fixed 64-byte field without a bounds check. The exploit scenario is specific and was reportedly reproduced under ASan with a stack-buffer-overflow at src/mqtt.c:240. This is a real, remotely exploitable memory-corruption vulnerability with RCE potential, not a theoretical best-practice concern or a mere crash (exclusion #16 does not apply since this is memory corruption, not a benign null/undefined crash). Actionable and high-signal.

filtered_findings.description: Subscribe/publish output is written into the fixed `client->wbuf` (allocated with exactly `conf->max_request_size` bytes) without ever comparing `c->towrite + len` against the buffer capacity. In subscribe_handler the retained message of the subscribed topic is memcpy'd at `c->wbuf + c->towrite` and `towrite` is advanced; the same unchecked pattern exists at handlers.c:227-228 (publish fan-out), 331-341 (session resume queue), 633-634 (SUBACK) and 767/811/830 (ACKs). An attacker can therefore cause a heap buffer overflow of the broker's write buffer.
filtered_findings.exploit_scenario: Reproduced locally under ASan: an unauthenticated client (no CONNECT at all) sends a PUBLISH with the RETAIN flag and a payload close to max_request_size (default 512KB) on topic 'a'. A second, normally authenticated client afterwards sends a SUBSCRIBE for 'a' (a single tuple is enough when the retained packet is near the buffer size; two tuples make it deterministic). subscribe_handler memcpy()s the 512KB retained packet into the victim's 512KB wbuf, producing 'AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... in subscribe_handler src/handlers.c:617' and broker death. Any memory-corruption primitive here is attacker controlled and can be leveraged toward code execution, not just a crash.
filtered_findings.recommendation: Before every write to `c->wbuf`, check that the packet size fits in the remaining capacity (`mqtt_size(...) <= conf->max_request_size - c->towrite`) and either flush/queue the output, disconnect the client, or drop the message otherwise. Do not size the write buffer from the same untrusted publish size without accounting for retained messages and batched SUBACKs.

_filter_metadata.justification: Concrete heap buffer overflow in C code (not Rust, so memory corruption is in scope). The finding identifies specific unchecked write locations (handlers.c:617 subscribe_handler, plus 227-228, 331-341, 633-634, 767/811/830) where retained message/publish data is memcpy'd into a fixed-size wbuf sized from untrusted publish length. Attack path is clear: unauthenticated PUBLISH with RETAIN fills a near-max_request_size retained packet, then a SUBSCRIBE triggers the overflow. ASan reproduction and specific remediation are provided, making this actionable for a security team.

filtered_findings.description: The broker only performs authentication inside connect_handler (handlers.c:366-375), but process_message() (server.c:867) dispatches every received packet to handle_command() without verifying `client->connected`/`client->session`. publish_handler, subscribe_handler and unsubscribe_handler never check connection state. Consequently, with `allow_anonymous false`, an unauthenticated socket can publish to arbitrary topics (including reserved `$SOL/...` topics) and a client whose CONNECT was rejected (CONNACK rc=4) remains connected and can keep sending commands.
filtered_findings.exploit_scenario: Reproduced locally with allow_anonymous=false and a password file: a socket that never sent CONNECT sends a PUBLISH packet (0x30) to topic 'topic'; an authenticated subscriber receives exactly the injected payload ('0x16\x00\x05topicINJECTED-UNAUTH'). The same primitive lets an attacker forge retained messages and spoof broker statistics (payload 'FAKE-STATS-99999' was delivered to a subscriber of $SOL/broker/uptime/). A SUBSCRIBE from such a socket instead crashes the broker because `e->client->session` is still NULL when subscriber_new() dereferences `s->session_id` (subscriber.c:45).
filtered_findings.recommendation: Enforce the state machine centrally: in process_message() (or handle_command) reject every packet type other than CONNECT while `client->connected == false`, and verify `client->session != NULL` before invoking subscribe/unsubscribe/puback/pubrec/pubcomp handlers. Also close the connection after a failed CONNECT instead of leaving it open.

_filter_metadata.justification: Concrete authentication bypass: with allow_anonymous=false, process_message dispatches PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE packets to handlers that never verify client->connected or client->session, so an unauthenticated socket can publish to arbitrary and reserved topics. The exploit scenario includes a local reproduction and specific code locations, making it actionable. The crash/DoS portion of the report is excluded per policy, but the core auth bypass remains a valid HIGH-severity vulnerability.

filtered_findings.description: The password-file generation utility hashes credentials with Python's `crypt.crypt(password)` without specifying a method or per-entry salt. On glibc this falls back to traditional DES crypt: a 2-character salt and only the first 8 characters of the password are significant, producing a 13-character, trivially brute-forceable hash. `check_passwd()` in src/util.c only verifies against whatever weak hash is stored.
filtered_findings.exploit_scenario: Anyone obtaining the generated password file (e.g., backup, misconfigured permissions, log/artifact copy) can recover the plaintext of most credentials within minutes on commodity hardware because DES crypt is limited to 8 significant characters with a 12-bit salt; passwords differing only after the 8th character collapse onto the same hash and authenticate successfully.
filtered_findings.recommendation: Generate hashes with a modern password-hashing scheme (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2id, e.g. `crypt.mksalt(crypt.METHOD_SHA512)` / `crypt.crypt(password, salt)` applied per entry) and reject/rehash legacy DES entries at startup.

_filter_metadata.justification: The finding describes a concrete weak password hashing issue: crypt.crypt(password) without an explicit method or salt defaults to traditional DES crypt on glibc, producing trivially brute-forceable 13-character hashes with only 8 significant password characters. If the generated password file is exposed, credentials can be recovered quickly. This is a real security weakness, not a theoretical best-practice concern.
